title: Watch: Dwarf Crocodiles Ambush Bats in a Pitch-Black Cave
summary:
Deep in the Abanda Caves of Gabon, in total darkness and surrounded by mounds of bat droppings, a group of dwarf crocodiles has been hiding a secret: they hunt bats. For the first time, scientists have captured video of these crocodiles sneaking up and snatching bats out of the air — a behavior never documented before.

Dwarf crocodiles (Osteolaemus tetraspis) are the world's smallest crocodile species, growing to only about 5 feet (1.5 meters) long. They're normally found in forests, rivers, and swamps across West and Central Africa. But this cave population, discovered in 2008, is different. They spend their days in complete darkness, stalking bat guano (excrement) in the remote Abanda Caves.

Researchers knew the crocs were eating bats and insects, but the animals refused to hunt when humans were around. "No matter how deeply in the bat guano I've been, or how long I've spent in the caves, whenever I'm in there, the crocodiles just aren't doing what they want to be doing," said Matt Shirley, a conservation ecologist and National Geographic Explorer who has studied the population for 15 years.

The new footage, captured with remote cameras for the National Geographic series "Africa: Earth's Wild Home," finally reveals their technique: a sneak attack.

Life in the cave is intense. The crocs navigate through guano that can be dry and fluffy or, after rain, a thick slurry. "Sometimes, to catch the crocodiles, I'm either literally standing with up to my neck in bat guano, or I'm having to lay down to crawl through tunnels," Shirley said. The acidic guano erodes their skin, giving them a distinct orange color.

But the cave has advantages: plenty of prey and few predators, so the crocs are often better fed than their forest relatives. Because they stay underground and mate only with each other, they're accumulating genetic differences that could help them adapt further. "It's very 'Jurassic Park,' you know — life-finds-a-way sort of a scenario," Shirley said. "This is evolution in action."
why_it_matters: This is evolution happening in front of scientists: a population cut off inside a cave begins to drift genetically from its relatives and could one day become a species of its own. It also shows how much we still miss about animals we think we understand — the behaviour stayed hidden for 15 years simply because the crocodiles refuse to hunt while people are watching.

background_read: Dwarf crocodiles (Osteolaemus tetraspis) are the smallest living crocodilians, and most of their populations live quietly in the forests, rivers and swamps of West and Central Africa. Scientists have found that they are more genetically varied than they first appeared, with some populations separated from one another for a very long time.

The cave population in the Abanda Caves was discovered in 2008 and has been studied for years by Matt Shirley, a conservation ecologist and National Geographic Explorer (a title given to scientists supported by the National Geographic Society). Gabon (a country on the Atlantic coast of Central Africa, largely covered in rainforest) has cave systems where bats roost in huge numbers, and the animals that move in afterwards build entire food webs on the droppings they leave behind.

Cave animals often evolve strange traits, such as pale skin or weak eyes, because they never see sunlight. The Abanda crocodiles are unusual: their orange colour comes from acidic guano damaging their skin rather than from lost pigment — a reminder that evolution produces whatever works in a particular environment.
The new footage was captured with remote cameras for the National Geographic series 'Africa: Earth's Wild Home'.

perspectives.description: For scientists, the footage is a breakthrough: it confirms a behaviour that had only been guessed at from stomach contents and tells them how these crocodiles hunt. It also proves that patient, long-term fieldwork and remote cameras can answer questions that direct observation cannot.

A population that lives in one cave system and breeds only with itself is fragile — if the cave, its bats or its water supply change, there is nowhere else for it to go. These researchers would argue the finding raises the stakes for protecting the Abanda Caves rather than just celebrating the video.

The cave crocodiles are a textbook example of how isolation starts the process of speciation: separated from forest relatives, they accumulate genetic differences and adapt to a strange environment. The orange skin caused by guano is a useful reminder that not every visible difference is an adaptation — some are simply damage from the surroundings.

DNA studies could soon show whether the cave crocodiles are a separate species rather than just an unusual group, which would directly affect how they are protected by law and conservation plans. If they are distinct, one small cave in Gabon could become a priority site for African wildlife protection.
